    <title>Unpacking the Compute Efficiency of Strong-to-Weak OPD against GRPO</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:47:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08453v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08453v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own rollouts under a frozen teacher's per-token supervision. Does this dense signal reduce the training FLOPs needed to reach a target accuracy compared with reinforcement learning? We systematically compare vanilla reverse-KL OPD with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) across task difficulty, student and teacher size, domain, and optimization choices, measuring held-out accuracy against training FLOPs. With an external post-trained teacher, OPD generally loses to GRPO in accuracy per training FLOP at matched settings, even when the teacher is further trained with GRPO, and often suffers response-length inflation. Yet a different teacher changes the picture: when the teacher is the student's own GRPO checkpoint, OPD recovers that checkpoint's accuracy on math with $50\times$ fewer distillation FLOPs than GRPO needs to reach the same accuracy. Following the same teacher setting, we consistently observe this high efficiency with a larger student, on code, and in a second model family. On a single domain, however, the GRPO checkpoint is already the desired model, so distilling it adds to total compute. Across domains, separate GRPO checkpoints hold different capabilities, and no single checkpoint serves every domain. Multi-teacher OPD (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) consolidates per-domain GRPO experts into a single student that matches each expert's accuracy, with the distillation stage costing only 5.2% (on 2 domains) and 8.0% (on 4 domains) of the specialist training FLOPs. Counting specialist training and distillation together, this pipeline reaches joint GRPO's performance on the 2-domain mix with 42.0% fewer total FLOPs.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08452v1</id>
    <title>ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:45:36Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08452v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08452v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08447v1</id>
    <title>Dynamical effects induced by synthetic SU(1,1) gauge fields</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:43:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08447v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08447v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Compact gauge fields are powerful tools for controlling quantum dynamics and topological phases of matter. Non-compact gauge fields are particularly relevant for open systems, where particles or energy are exchanged with the environment. Here, we investigate the wavepacket and entanglement dynamics induced by an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field. The wavepacket undergoes non-Abelian non-compact Bloch oscillations, in which the spectrum of an auxiliary one-dimensional quantum problem determines the transition between stable oscillations and unstable amplification. In the unstable adiabatic regime, the wavepacket probes an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ topological defect, and its amplification is determined solely by a hyperbolic solid angle in Minkowski space. Threading an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field through a bosonic tight-binding model yields the bosonic Kitaev model, whose volume or super-volume entanglement scaling is governed by the stability of the gauge field. We further propose an experimental realization of an $\mathrm{SU}(1,1)$ gauge field in a spinor condensate. Our results can be generalized to other non-compact groups and higher dimensions, providing a geometric framework for entanglement control, selective amplification, and engineering energy transfer.</summary>

    <title>A Hidden Markov Preference Model for Online Prediction of Adversary Actions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:37:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08445v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08445v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A defender anticipating an attacker needs a probability distribution over the attacker's next action from information available before that action occurs. Two structures complicate this: the attacker's behavioral regime persists and can switch within an episode, and each action combines an operation with state-dependent arguments whose feasible values change over time. We capture both with a hidden Markov model whose latent state is the active regime and whose regime-conditioned action law is defined on a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions. The same likelihood forms the next-action distribution and updates the regime belief once the action is seen, and a partially observed prefix contributes its resolved local factors. Estimation separates into convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabeled. We derive a reach-weighted nodewise KL expression for regime information, a sequence-wise log-loss bound for switching regime paths, and a uniform fallback guarantee. On the CAGE 2 cyber defense benchmark the filtered latent state is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after a controller switch the loss begins to fall in three steps against ten for a recurrent baseline.</summary>

    <title>Polynomial-time classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:36:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08444v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08444v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Sampling experiments are a leading approach to demonstrating quantum computational advantage, yet their robustness to experimental noise is not completely understood. We develop a common framework for classical simulation of boson and fermion sampling under thermal loss, including pure loss. For Fock-state boson sampling, Gaussian boson sampling with fixed uniform squeezing, and fermion sampling with magic inputs, we obtain polynomial-time sampling at inverse-polynomial total variation error, for any fixed nonzero overall loss rate, and with high probability over Haar-random interferometers. A milder flatness assumption on the ideal output distribution suffices for quasipolynomial-time simulation without Haar randomness. With constant thermal loss per layer, the same flatness assumption gives polynomial-time simulation at logarithmic depth. Our bounds for Fock-state boson sampling cover both dilute and saturated regimes and become stronger near full input filling: when only a bounded number of input modes are empty, the noisy output for Haar-random interferometers converges, as the number of modes grows, to a distribution independent of the interferometer.</summary>

    <title>Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:31:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08439v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08439v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies, produced by three separate processes and checked for overlap with the training data, with five candidates per question and, for eight of them, also with eighteen. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (English-derived jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release is more accurate in every setting, by up to 0.24. Eleven of these fourteen gains survive a Holm correction (slang with eighteen candidates and descriptive sentences with five do not), and for jargon on all labels the label-level interval excludes zero in both settings. On abbreviations and opaque codes it gives no usable gain: on abbreviations it is not better, and worse on the clean slice, and on opaque codes both releases stay at or below chance once labels related to training options are removed. In most cells where accuracy rises, the risk-coverage area falls, but with eighteen candidates confident errors rise on jargon and slang. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.</summary>

    <title>Understanding AI from the Inside: The State of Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:30:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08438v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08438v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from surveyed methods, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.</summary>

    <title>DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:28:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08434v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08434v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Designing protein sequences that satisfy both secondary structure requirements and solubility targets remains challenging. We present DiffSequence-Q, a hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on secondary structure at each residue and a continuous solubility target. To introduce quantum auxiliary supervision during training, we employ a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations. The auxiliary prediction loss is jointly optimized with the diffusion objective, allowing quantum auxiliary supervision to influence the learned denoising model. Once trained, protein sequences are generated entirely through classical reverse diffusion. On the CATH benchmark, DiffSequence-Q achieved the highest secondary structure recovery among the four evaluated models for complete sequence generation. Evaluation with a separately trained solubility prediction model showed that the best QNN and QKAN configurations achieved mean predicted solubility scores 14.0% and 22.7% higher than the multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline, respectively. Experimental characterization further demonstrated biological activity across three distinct protein families. Selected defensins exhibited pronounced inhibitory activity against Aspergillus niger, while xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases exhibited substantial enzymatic activity. Together, these results support DiffSequence-Q as a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with experimentally demonstrated biological activity.</summary>

    <title>MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:27:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08433v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08433v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.</summary>

    <title>The Power of Meta Access in the Software of the Future --- Demonstrated on LLM Chat UIs and Chat AI</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:22:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08428v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08428v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. Yet the model sees the current dialogue but not the workspace around it. We explore meta access---giving the assistant a structured, permissioned view of the interface itself and propose a ladder of levels: feature tutoring; metadata, settings, and preference access; retrieval over summaries and messages, confirmed mutation, and full orchestration. Meta access can turn a chat client from many screens into one entry point for finding, navigating, organising, and operating it, while raising risks around grounding, privacy, prompt injection, and trust. General-purpose agentic harnesses are runtimes; because they can change their own settings, meta access becomes reflexive and needs a separate control-plane boundary. We ground this in the Meta Chat prototype of the Chat AI client. It builds bounded context from, e.g., summaries, settings, and relevant messages; links references to conversations, topics, and personas; supports confirmed, reversible changes; offers a browsable tutorial library; and recommends personas as user-started conversations. By exposing application state in structured form, meta access can extend screen readers from widget descriptions to semantic workspace operations. Meta access thus turns chat from a window onto one conversation into a control layer for the whole workspace, extending chat toward agentic capability without surrendering user control. As assistants become embedded in IDEs, dashboards, office suites, and operating systems, AI-era interfaces should expose a structured, permissioned model of their state and capabilities, ideally by opening their existing metamodels through a debugger-like interface.</summary>

    <title>Quantum enhanced beam displacement estimation: sensitivity limits, optimal probes, and measurement schemes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:22:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08427v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08427v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We investigate the ultimate sensitivity limits for measuring small transverse beam displacements and identify optimal strategies that attain them, using the framework of mode parameter estimation. We contrast two families of states with different resource constraints, using Hermite-Gauss and Laguerre-Gauss mode pairs. First, for fixed total photon number states, the optimal state is identified and we show that it asymptotically approaches a rotated NOON state. The sensitivity bound is compared to that of an asymptotically optimal pure Gaussian state with fixed average photon number. Finally, we propose concrete measurement schemes using the method of moments and show that the twin-Fock state may provide a viable alternative to the rotated NOON state for this task. Our work provides a broader benchmark for developing practical strategies for spatial sensing at the quantum limit.</summary>

    <title>Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models Via Calibrated Latent Probing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:21:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08425v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08425v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely, calibrated, and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug, a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86% of runs, versus at most 21% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at https://vla-tug.github.io.</summary>

    <title>Disorder-blind Mpemba acceleration of quantum state preparation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:20:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08424v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08424v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Using the strong Mpemba effect to accelerate relaxation by initial-state design requires suppressing the slowest mode, which typically needs prior knowledge of the system. However, in disordered systems, this mode is sample-dependent, so a fixed preparation generally retains a slow-mode overlap. We show that a ``blind'' preparation, designed from the clean chain without knowledge of the disorder realisation or its distribution, can start farther from stationarity yet overtake a reference in typical samples of a dephased disordered XX chain. It requires only the chain geometry and the particle number. At strong dephasing, the density dynamics maps to a resistor chain, and an exact inverse-generator identity links the residual overlap to the spatial resistance profile. We find two distinct thresholds: a finite mean resistance suffices for diffusion, but the residual overlap decays as $L^{-1/2}$ with chain length $L$ only when the resistance variance is finite; rare weak links slow this decay. We predict the fraction of samples in which the blind preparation wins, which is an ensemble-level measure of its reliability. Finite-size calculations support both scaling regimes with interactions at strong dephasing. We give preparation circuits and a density readout for the residual overlap.</summary>

    <title>Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:19:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08421v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08421v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Discovering continuous symmetries directly from differential-equation data can reveal geometric structure for model reduction and scientific machine learning without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form representation of the governing system. We formulate intrinsic Lie point-symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem on sampled jet-space data. Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator and separated from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions. The framework combines prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients. A rank-stabilization preflight test diagnoses systems whose represented intrinsic symmetry algebra does not stabilize under dictionary refinement. On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain. Here we show that explicit intrinsic continuous-symmetry generators can be recovered from data obtained from exact or approximate differential systems.</summary>

    <title>On the limitations of molecular representations</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:19:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08420v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08420v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Molecular representations such as fingerprints and learned embeddings play a central role in cheminformatics and small-molecule machine learning. They serve as the primary input for a diverse array of tasks, including clustering, dataset splitting, and virtual screening, yet their evaluation is often limited to downstream model performance on narrow benchmark tasks. We carried out a systematic investigation of the quality of molecular representations, finding that none of the state-of-the-art molecular embedding models capture graph structure, 3D shape, or ADMET endpoint similarity better than fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors. However, classical fingerprints also revealed their own material limitations. For example, we show that depending on the representation, between 225M and $\sim$4B molecules have non-unique representations in the 10.8B Enamine REAL database, with implications for virtual screening. Our findings provide an insight into the current limitations of molecular representations, outlining future research directions for the development of more robust encodings of small molecules.</summary>

    <title>Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:18:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08417v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08417v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958).
  We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves.
  More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.</summary>

    <title>Spectral and Subspace Dynamics of LoRA in Supervised Fine-Tuning and Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:17:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08414v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08414v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is commonly used in both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), often under similar optimizer settings. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.</summary>

    <title>The Gold Rush in AI4Math, II: What are signatures of AI-assisted Proofs?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:17:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08412v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08412v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The growing use of AI in mathematics raises a question: can we detect AI involvement in proofs, separately from AI assistance with writing? Historical arXiv papers, recent papers disclosing substantive AI use, and manuscripts released by OpenAI provide a rich empirical basis for studying this question. However, several challenges remain: lack of matched case-control pairs; potential incompleteness of disclosure; and lack of ready-to-use features designed to capture signals of AI involvement in proofs.
  To address these challenges, we construct five cohorts comprising 8,281 papers by combining existing manuscripts with those we produced using generative AI. These cohorts span different levels of AI involvement and include matched pairs of papers addressing the same research problems. We then introduce ProofTrace, a framework that represents each paper as a graph of immediate proof support (GIPS) and extracts interpretable features of mathematical organization.
  Our study yields three discoveries. First, principal-component projections of our features reveal a qualitative gradient of AI involvement, where AI-reworded papers remain close to human papers, the two AI-generated cohorts depart in broadly shared directions, and papers disclosing substantive AI use occupy intermediate positions which shifts toward AI-generated cohorts over time. Second, we identify recurring signatures of AI-generated proofs, such as fewer externally cited results, greater reliance on intermediate conclusions, and altered graph connectivity; many of these signatures persist under controls for research field, manuscript length, or graph size. Finally, in a separate detection experiment, ProofTrace distinguishes human-written papers from those disclosing substantive AI use. Its performance remains stable under AI rewording, whereas the performance of state-of-the-art text-based detectors declines sharply.</summary>

    <title>Conformal Prediction for Time-Dependent PDEs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:15:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08409v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08409v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Uncertainty quantification is crucial in scientific machine learning, where models inform safety-critical tasks such as flood forecasting, financial risk management, and thermal control in machines. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees, but in time-dependent settings common to physics and engineering, these guarantees can break down, leading to systematic undercoverage. We study this problem in the context of surrogate models for time-dependent physical systems described by partial differential equations. We prove that in a function space setting, distributions at arbitrarily close times can be mutually singular, making exact coverage guarantees impossible. We further show that in discretized settings, the total variation distance between distributions often saturates exponentially fast with the grid resolution, mandating restrictions on the spatial discretization to ensure coverage. Finally, for certain settings, we show how to use principled weighted conformal prediction to obtain finite-sample coverage guarantees over growing time horizons.</summary>

    <summary>Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world.     <title>StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:12:49Z</updated>

    <summary>Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency.</summary>

    <title>Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:08:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08396v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08396v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Erbium-doped solids like $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ have properties that make them suitable for quantum-network memories, however, their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence. Operating at Zero First-Order Zeeman (ZEFOZ) points allows us to mitigate this, where we evaluate the ZEFOZ landscape for Site-2 $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ by incorporating a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian treatment with the anisotropic magnetic-field covariance derived from the native $^{89}\mathrm{Y}$ crystal lattice directly. Operating-point screening criteria were adopted to devise a Pareto-optimal frontier of four transition pairs to balance modeled Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}$) against microwave control authority. The $ε_{14}\leftrightarrowε_{15}$ transition exhibits the longest modeled Y-bath-induced quadratic pure-dephasing time, $T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}>2.2\times10^5~\mathrm{s}$, while the $ε_{12}\leftrightarrowε_{13}$ transition stood out, achieving a Rabi frequency coefficient of $1.248 \times 10^5~\mathrm{Hz/mT}$. An assumption-based Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis demonstrates that while uncompensated deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition away from its nominal magnetic-field coordinate, the shifted operating points can be recovered via numerical vector-field recalibration. The Pareto-optimal coordinates were mathematically recovered for all sampled Hamiltonian perturbations, and the $84.1^{\mathrm{st}}$-percentile field relocations ranged from $10.95$ to $27.97~\mathrm{mT}$. The intended operation near $10~\mathrm{mK}$ must be taken into account for the suppression of Er-induced spectral diffusion through electronic-spin polarization, while the extended Y-bath pure-dephasing timescales also remain conditional on the adopted temporal-correlation model.</summary>

    <title>Synthesis of Ovarian Cancer Multi-Omics Datasets: A Biology-Informed Evaluation Framework</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:07:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08394v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08394v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, motivating synthetic cohorts as a complementary resource. As generative model development accelerates, we shift the focus from proposing yet another architecture to defining evaluation criteria that determine whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure. We introduce a biology-informed and patient-disjoint framework for evaluating the generation of paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and apply it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort. The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and coherence between RNA and CNV pairs using agreement between real training and held-out data as a reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics. We adapt three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders to generate paired profiles. The model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity. The protocol and case study offer the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08392v1</id>
    <title>Learning a patient world model for health system simulation in intensive care</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:06:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08392v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08392v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Designing healthcare strategies requires anticipating their clinical and operational consequences before implementation, a task that often relies on health system simulation. Such a simulation necessitates modeling how patient states evolve and generate care demands. However, conventional approaches typically tailor compact state transitions to a single policy question and omit history-dependent dynamics, thus requiring the redefinition of states and transitions when there is a new question that entails different clinical information. We propose to learn a patient world model from longitudinal EHRs using a neural network to provide a shared clinical representation of patient trajectories that can serve simulation questions across scenarios. Taking ICU operations as an example, we train the model on MIMIC-IV, freeze it, and couple its time-queryable predictions to shared ICU calendars, resources, and queues via scenario-specific mappings, so that one model renders admission demand, care tasks, and discharge proposals across simulations evaluating ICU bed capacity, care dispatch, and post-ICU transfer capacity. Experiments show that our model matches Markov and semi-Markov comparators in aggregate occupancy and directional responses to capacity and dispatch policies. It also reproduces policy gains from replayed observed trajectories. For patients entering the same support state from different prior trajectories, the learned representation captures a 24-h recovery difference (-6.4 predicted versus -6.7 observed percentage points), a contrast missed by compact state models, which propagates into distinct simulated care demand, queue burden, and bed use. These results indicate that a learned world model of patient dynamics has the potential to replace question-specific state models, allowing new care policies to be evaluated by reconfiguring the scenario without model rebuilding.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08386v1</id>
    <title>Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:04:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08386v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08386v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08383v1</id>
    <title>FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:00:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08383v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08383v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Federated learning servers combine client models with a fixed aggregation rule, and each rule in common use is designed for one kind of heterogeneity. We study whether a large language model (LLM) that inspects the client models can choose the rule itself, without any training on the server. In FedReason, the LLM is called every ten rounds. It analyses the weights by running code in a restricted server-side sandbox, sees only the printed results, may score a few candidates on a 500-image proxy set, and submits a short Python aggregation program. The server applies the program until the next call and falls back to FedAvg whenever its output is invalid. Full weight tensors never leave the server. We evaluated FedReason with Claude Opus 5.5 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with ResNet-18 under Dirichlet label skew, width-heterogeneous sub-models and Byzantine clients, in 168 runs against 14 baselines. Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points. It was the strongest server-side rule on CIFAR-100 but did not beat SCAFFOLD, which changes client training. With three of ten clients malicious, it excluded all sign-flipping clients from the first round and stayed about one point below FLTrust without training a root model. Without proxy feedback, accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed. A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08379v1</id>
    <title>Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T17:56:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08379v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08379v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08376v1</id>
    <title>Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T17:53:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08376v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08376v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08372v1</id>
    <title>MOMASPLAT: Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T17:50:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08372v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08372v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MOMASPLAT, a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multiview observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MOMASPLAT combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MOMASPLAT on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MOMASPLAT substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for largescale real-world data collection.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08369v1</id>
    <title>NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T17:48:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08369v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08369v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.</summary>

For example, preliminary human trials examining the fasting mimicking diet (very low-calorie, low-protein diet 1-week per month) or short term fasting (48-120 hours (h)), known as periodic fasting, surrounding chemotherapy may increase effectiveness of treatment and decrease side effects related to chemotherapy. Yet these diets have low adherence, side effects of their own, and may increase patient burden and decrease quality of life. In contrast, time restricted eating (TRE) is a form of intermittent fasting with high adherence that may have similar positive effects on treatment outcomes without the untoward side-effects. The Mediterranean diet has also been shown to improve patient and treatment outcomes in this population. The additive effect might be even more beneficial. We aim to test the safety and feasibility of 8-h TRE compared to TRE combined with a mediterranean style diet among female breast cancer patients initiating chemotherapy for stage I-III breast cancer. The safety of this treatment will also be studied.","detailedDescription":"Before treatment starts, patients will have a complete exam, including medical history and documentation of disease, blood, and marrow tests. A chest x-ray will be taken. CT scans may be taken if needed. A bone marrow sample will be taken through a large needle. An EKG and MUGA (heart function tests) will be performed.

During treatment, patients will give blood samples (about 1 tablespoon each) at least twice a week. A bone marrow sample will be repeated 2 and 3 weeks from the beginning of treatment to check on response. After two courses of chemotherapy, the tests done before treatment will be repeated to check for response.

All patients will receive 2 kinds of chemotherapy courses for a total of 8 courses. Chemotherapy courses will be given through a large vein by a central venous catheter (a plastic tube usually placed under the collarbone). Imatinib mesylate will be given as a pill with the chemotherapy.

Course 1 will start with cyclophosphamide given by vein over 2-3 hours every 12 hours for 6 doses over 3 days (Days 1,2,3). Mesna will be given by vein continuously for 4 days with the cyclophosphamide to protect the bladder. Doxorubicin will be given by vein over 24 hours on Day 4. Vincristine will be given by short infusion on Days 4 and 11. Dexamethasone (a steroid) will be given by mouth or by vein on Days 1-4 and 11-14. The imatinib mesylate will be given by mouth with breakfast and a large glass of water daily on Days 1-14. Medicines will be given to prevent nausea and to protect the kidneys from increased amounts of uric acid, which may be released when leukemia cells die.

G-CSF (growth stimulating colony factor) will be given after completion of the chemotherapy. It is given to allow for rapid recovery of the normal marrow. G-CSF will be injected under the skin until the counts recover. Treatment to the brain will be given inside the spinal fluid with methotrexate around Day 2 and cytarabine about day 7. This is done to prevent the leukemia from developing there.

For patients aged 60 years or older, this Course 1 will be given in a protective isolation room to decrease the risk of infection(s).

During Course 2, patients will be given methotrexate by infusion over 24 hours on the first day and cytarabine at a high dose over 2 hours every 12 hours for 4 doses (Days 2 and 3). Citrovorum factor (leucovorin), an antidote for side effects of methotrexate, will be given by vein or by mouth for 2-3 days (Day 2 and on). Solumedrol (a steroid) will be given by vein every 12 hours for 6 doses. Imatinib mesylate will be given by mouth with breakfast and a large glass of water on Days 1-14 or daily, depending on tolerance with Course 1. G-CSF will be given as in Course 1. The treatment to the brain inside the spinal fluid will be given as in Course 1 around Days 2 and 7.

The chemotherapy will alternate between hyper-CVAD plus imatinib mesylate (Courses 1, 3, 5, and 7) and methotrexate/cytarabine plus imatinib mesylate (Courses 2, 4, 6, and 8) to complete a total of 8 courses. G-CSF will be given as in Course 1. Anti-nausea medicine will be given with each course of chemotherapy. The urine will be alkalized to protect the kidneys. Antibiotics will be given by mouth to prevent infection.

After the 8 courses, monthly maintenance chemotherapy plus imatinib mesylate will be given. This includes daily imatinib mesylate, monthly vincristine by vein, and prednisone by mouth for 5 days every month. Maintenance chemotherapy will be given for a total of 24 months, and will be interrupted by 2 periods of intensive chemotherapy courses with hyper-CVAD and imatinib mesylate at 6 and 13 months from the start of maintenance. Imatinib mesylate will be continued daily as tolerated indefinitely.

After two courses of the intensive chemotherapy, the response to the treatment will be evaluated. If the leukemia is responding, the therapy will be continued. Patients will be taken off study if the leukemia starts to get worse.

During and after completion of treatment, patients will have a complete exam, including blood tests. If needed, a chest X-ray or CT scan will be done. A bone marrow sample will be taken through a large needle. Patients will then return every 2 to 3 months for a checkup, including blood and bone marrow. X-rays and heart studies (MUGA or ECG) may be repeated if needed.

An Ommaya reservoir may also be placed surgically as a route to treat leukemia in the brain or to prevent leukemia in patients who have difficulty with the spinal treatments. An Ommaya reservoir is an access port inserted under the skin of the scalp that enters into the spinal fluid cavity of the brain.

Treatment will be given on an inpatient basis (3 to 5 days) for the 8 intensive courses of chemotherapy, or as indicated by the clinical condition. The maintenance treatments will be given as an outpatient, except for the courses of hyper-CVAD and imatinib mesylate.

This is an investigational study. The FDA has approved imatinib mesylate for use in chronic myelogenous leukemia and other clinical research studies. About 55 patients will take part in this study. 1. Histologically or cytologically confirmed recurrent or metastatic sarcoma that is measurable.
2. Adequate hepatic function: Total bilirubin \< 2.0 mg/dL (upper limit included); AST/ALT \< 2x institutional norm; alkaline phosphatase \< 2.5x upper limit of institutional norm unless the patient has extensive bone metastases. Patients with elevated alkaline phosphatase due to extensive liver disease will be excluded from study; albumin \> 3.0 mg/dL. There must be no substantial ascites. PT and PTT must be within normal limits.
3. Performance status must be \< 1 (ECOG 0-1) with a life expectancy of at least 3 months.
4. Hemoglobin \> 9 gms%
5. Absolute granulocyte count \> 1000/uL, and platelet count \> 100,000/uL.
6. Serum creatinine of less than 1.5 mg%.
7. There must be no plans for the patient to receive further cancer therapy from the date of enrollment until the completion of the 6-week follow-up visit.
8. Accessibility of peripheral or central IV line
9. Age \> 10 years
10. Patients will be off chemotherapy for a minimum of 4 weeks prior to initiation of therapy and should have recovered to Grade 1 or less toxicity.
11. The ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent document.

Exclusion Criteria:

related fatigue in cancer survivors.","detailedDescription":"Cancer-related fatigue (CRF) is a distressing, persistent and subjective sense of physical, emotional, or cognitive tiredness related to cancer or its treatment. Currently there is a lack of effective conventional pharmacological intervention for treating this condition. Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) could be alternative therapy for managing CRF.

This study is a phase 2, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial to examine the efficacy and safety of a TCM decoction, the modified Xiang Bei Yang Rong Tang (XBYRT) in alleviating CRF in cancer survivors. Study participants recruited from National Cancer Centre Singapore (NCCS) will be randomized to receive either the XBYRT or placebo decoction. Participants will take their assigned decoction daily for a duration of 8 weeks and will be assessed using patient reported outcome (PRO) questionnaires. PROs used are the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC-QLQ 30) for QOL, the Multidimensional Fatigue Symptom Inventory Short Form (MFSI-SF) for fatigue and Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-Cognitive Function (FACT-Cog) Version 3 for cognitive abilities. The changes in scores measured by these assessment tools will be compared between the XBYRT intervention and placebo groups. Blood biomarkers such as inflammatory cytokines, mitochondrial DNA and oxidative stress markers will also be evaluated in the study participants. Additionally, adverse events or serious adverse events in participants will be monitored for safety.

Results from this study will provide a better understanding on the role of TCM in managing CRF."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Cancer","Fatigue","Cognitive Impairment"],"keywords":["Cancer","Cancer Related Fatigue","Cognitive Impairment","Survivorship","Traditional Chinese Medicine"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["PHASE2"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"PARALLEL","primaryPurpose":"TREATMENT","maskingInfo":{"masking":"QUADRUPLE","whoMasked":["PARTICIPANT","CARE_PROVIDER","INVESTIGATOR","OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR"]}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":80,"type":"ESTIMATED"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"XBYRT decoction","type":"EXPERIMENTAL","description":"Participants assigned to receive the modifed Xiang Bei Yang Rong Tang granules","interventionNames":["Other: Modified Xiang Bei Yang Rong Tang"]},{"label":"Placebo","type":"PLACEBO_COMPARATOR","description":"Participants assigned to receive placebo (contains 5% of XBYRT) granules","interventionNames":["Other: Placebo"]}],"interventions":[{"type":"OTHER","name":"Modified Xiang Bei Yang Rong Tang","description":"Modified Xiang Bei Yang Rong Tang is a combination of 15 herbal components and it is available in granules form to be dissolved in hot water for consumption","armGroupLabels":["XBYRT decoction"]},{"type":"OTHER","name":"Placebo","description":"Placebo granules contain 5% XBYRT, colourant, bitterant and 95% starch filler","armGroupLabels":["Placebo"]}]},"outcomesModule":{"primaryOutcomes":[{"measure":"Difference in Global Health Status (GHS) score","description":"Difference in Global Health Status (GHS) score from the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ-C30) between XBYRT interventional and placebo arms from baseline to 8 weeks after baseline.
